content: Tramadol is an opioid analgesic that is approved for managing moderate to severe pain. It is considered to have a lower potential for abuse compared to stronger opioids like morphine, which is why it is subject to less stringent regulatory controls. Tramadol is often considered as a step 2 option in the World Health Organization (WHO) analgesic ladder for pain management. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and adverse effects of tramadol, either alone or in combination with paracetamol (acetaminophen), for the treatment of cancer-related pain. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, as well as three clinical trial registries. The last search was performed on November 2, 2016. The inclusion criteria required randomized studies with either placebo or active controls, involving at least 10 participants per treatment group. Both blinded and open studies were included, but non-randomized studies, case reports, clinical observations, and studies of experimental pain were excluded. Two independent reviewers extracted data using a standardized form, ensuring agreement before entering the data into Review Manager 5. The extracted data included participant demographics, cancer type, drug regimens, study design, duration, follow-up, pain outcomes, adverse events, and withdrawal rates. Multiple reports of the same study were consolidated to treat each study as a single unit of analysis. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and a 'Summary of findings' table was created. Key outcomes of interest included pain reduction of 30% or greater and 50% or greater from baseline, participants reporting pain no worse than mild, and participants feeling much or very much improved. The review included 10 studies (12 reports) with a total of 958 adult participants. All participants had chronic cancer-related pain of moderate to severe intensity, with most reporting pain levels of at least 4/10 despite current treatment. The participants' ages ranged from 24 to 87 years, with mean ages between 59 and 70 years. The study durations varied from one day to six months, and five studies used a cross-over design. Tramadol doses ranged from 50 mg as a single dose to 600 mg per day, with 300-400 mg per day being the most common dosing range. Nine of the studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in one to four criteria, and the overall quality of evidence was deemed very low. This was due to issues such as lack of blinding in outcome assessments, poorly described methods for sequence generation and allocation concealment, and small sample sizes. Reporting of important outcomes was often inadequate. The studies included eight different active comparators and one placebo comparison, but the available data were insufficient to draw firm conclusions for any outcome. Some specific comparisons included oral tramadol versus codeine plus paracetamol, dihydrocodeine, and rectal versus oral tramadol, but these provided no data for key outcomes. One study involved tramadol combined with paracetamol, but only four participants received this intervention. Another study compared tramadol with flupirtine, a drug that is no longer available. A further study compared tramadol with placebo and a combination of cobrotoxin, tramadol, and ibuprofen, but the dosing schedule was poorly described. Two studies (191 participants) compared tramadol with buprenorphine, and one study (131 participants) reported a similar proportion of participants experiencing no or mild pain at 14 days. Three studies (300 participants) compared tramadol with morphine. In one study, a group combining tramadol, tramadol plus paracetamol, and paracetamol plus codeine as a single weak-opioid group reported a 30% pain reduction in 47% of participants (55/117), compared to 82% (91/110) with morphine. A 50% pain reduction was achieved in 42% of participants (49/117) in the weak-opioid group, compared to 75% (83/110) with morphine. No useful information was available for other outcomes related to benefits or harms. The authors concluded that there is limited, very low-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials suggesting that tramadol may provide pain relief in some adults with cancer-related pain. There is no evidence available for its use in children. The evidence also suggests that tramadol is less effective than morphine. The review does not provide a reliable indication of the likely effects of tramadol, and there is a high likelihood that the actual effects could differ substantially. The role of tramadol in managing cancer pain and its position as a step 2 option in the WHO analgesic ladder remains unclear.
